subject: maths
title: Chapter 2 · Test 1
summary: Chapter 2 test 1: parallel lines, triangle angle sums, quadrilateral properties, and interior and exterior angles of polygons.
body: This test covers Chapter 2: angles and parallel lines, angle sums of triangles, properties of quadrilaterals, interior angles of polygons and exterior angles. It has 15 questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes. Work with no notes and no calculator unless the question says. Diagrams are drawn to scale, but always use the angle rules and the facts you are given — never measure. Write your working, give a reason for each step, and check that your answer is the angle the question asks for (not just the value of x).

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD and ∠APQ = 72°. Find x, the size of ∠PQD, in the diagram.
questions.explanation: x and the 72° angle are between the parallel lines on opposite sides of the transversal, so they are alternate angles and are equal. 108 comes from treating them as co-interior (adding to 180°).
steps: The two angles are between AB and CD, on opposite sides of PQ — they are alternate angles (Z shape).
Alternate angles on parallel lines are equal.
So x = 72.

mistakes.B: Step 2: alternate angles are equal — they do not add to 180°. Look for the Z shape.
mistakes.C: Step 2: there is no right angle here, so do not subtract from 90°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: alternate angles are equal — do not double the angle.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD cut by a transversal at P and Q. Angle APQ is 72° and angle PQD is marked x

questions.prompt: In the diagram, side BC of triangle ABC is extended to D. Find x.
questions.explanation: The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles: 47 + 68 = 115. 65° is the interior angle at C, not the exterior one.
steps: x is the exterior angle at C; the interior opposite angles are at A (47°) and B (68°).
Exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 65° is the angle inside the triangle at C. x is the exterior angle next to it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the exterior angle equals the sum of BOTH interior opposite angles, 47° + 68°, not 180° − 47°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the exterior angle equals the sum of BOTH interior opposite angles, 47° + 68°, not 180° − 68°.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with angle A = 47° and angle B = 68°. Side BC is extended past C to D, and the exterior angle ACD is marked x

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a nonagon (9 sides). What is the sum of its interior angles?
questions.explanation: From one vertex a nonagon splits into 9 − 2 = 7 triangles, so the angle sum is 7 × 180 = 1260°. 1620° uses 9 triangles instead of 7.
steps: A nonagon has n = 9 sides.
From one vertex it splits into 9 − 2 = 7 triangles.

mistakes.A: Step 2: use n − 2 triangles, not n. A nonagon splits into 7 triangles from one vertex.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the number of triangles is n − 2 = 7, not n − 1 = 8.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 360° is the angle sum of a quadrilateral only. Use (n − 2) × 180°.

questions.diagram_alt: A regular nonagon: a shape with 9 equal sides

questions.prompt: ABCDEF is a regular hexagon. Side AB is extended past B. Find the exterior angle x.
questions.explanation: The 6 equal exterior angles of a regular hexagon add to 360°, so each is 360 ÷ 6 = 60°. 120° is the interior angle, not the exterior one.
steps: The exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360°.
A regular hexagon has 6 equal exterior angles.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 120° is the interior angle. x is the exterior angle, the turn at the corner.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the exterior angles add to 360°, not 180°, so divide 360 by 6.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 360° is the total of all six exterior angles — share it between the 6 corners.

questions.diagram_alt: Regular hexagon ABCDEF with side AB extended past B (dashed). The exterior angle between the extension and side BC is marked x

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD. Use the corresponding angles in the diagram to find x.
questions.explanation: Corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal, so 2x + 25 = 115, giving 2x = 90 and x = 45. Setting them to add to 180 (x = 20) treats them as co-interior.
steps: The two angles are in the same position at each crossing (F shape) — corresponding angles, so they are equal: 2x + 25 = 115.
Subtract 25 from both sides: 2x = 90.
Divide both sides by 2: x = 45 (check: 2 × 45 + 25 = 115 ✓).

mistakes.A: Step 2: subtract 25 from both sides (115 − 25 = 90), do not add it.
mistakes.C: Step 1: corresponding angles are equal, so write 2x + 25 = 115 — do not make them add to 180.
mistakes.D: Step 2: subtract the 25 first, then divide by 2. 115 ÷ 2 ignores the + 25.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD cut by a transversal at P and Q. Above AB on the right of the transversal the angle is (2x + 25)°; above CD on the right of the transversal the angle is 115°

questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and ∠ABC = 64°. Find ∠BAC.
questions.explanation: AB = AC, so the base angles at B and C are both 64°, and ∠BAC = 180 − 64 − 64 = 52°. 116° only subtracts one base angle.
steps: AB = AC, so the angles opposite them are equal: ∠ACB = ∠ABC = 64°.
Angle sum of a triangle: the three angles add to 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 64° is a base angle, not the apex. Do not halve 180 − 64; both base angles are 64°.
mistakes.B: Step 2: there are TWO base angles of 64°. Subtract both from 180.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the equal angles are the base angles at B and C (opposite the equal sides), not the angle at A.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with AB and AC marked equal. Angle ABC is 64° and angle BAC is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCD is a parallelogram with ∠ABC = (2x + 30)° and ∠BCD = (x + 15)°. Find ∠ADC.
questions.explanation: ∠ABC and ∠BCD are co-interior (AB ∥ DC), so 3x + 45 = 180 and x = 45. Then ∠ABC = 120°, and ∠ADC is opposite it, so ∠ADC = 120°. 60° is ∠BCD, the angle next to it.
steps: ∠ABC and ∠BCD lie along side BC between parallel sides, so they are co-interior: 2x + 30 + x + 15 = 180.
Collect like terms: 3x + 45 = 180, so 3x = 135 and x = 45. Then ∠ABC = 2 × 45 + 30 = 120°.
Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so ∠ADC = ∠ABC = 120°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 60° is ∠BCD. ∠ADC is opposite ∠ABC, so it equals ∠ABC.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 45 is the value of x. Substitute it back to find the angle.
mistakes.C: Step 1: a parallelogram does not have to have right angles. Use co-interior angles to write an equation.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallelogram ABCD. Angle ABC is (2x + 30)°, angle BCD is (x + 15)°, and angle ADC is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: The pentagon in the diagram has angles 110°, 95°, 125°, x° and x°. Find x.
questions.explanation: A pentagon's angles add to (5 − 2) × 180 = 540°. The known angles add to 330°, so 2x = 210 and x = 105. 210 forgets to share between the two equal angles.
steps: Pentagon angle sum = (5 − 2) × 180 = 540°.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 210 is the two x angles together. Divide by 2.
mistakes.C: Step 1: a pentagon's angles add to 540°, not 360° (that is a quadrilateral).
mistakes.D: Step 1: a pentagon makes 5 − 2 = 3 triangles, so its angle sum is 540°, not 720°.

questions.diagram_alt: Pentagon ABCDE with interior angles A = 110°, B = 95°, C = 125°, D = x° and E = x°

questions.prompt: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 144°. How many sides does it have?
questions.explanation: The exterior angle is 180 − 144 = 36°, and n = 360 ÷ 36 = 10 sides. Dividing 360 by 144 gives 2.5, which is not a whole number of sides.
steps: Exterior angle = 180 − 144 = 36° (interior and exterior make a straight line).
The equal exterior angles add to 360°, so n = 360 ÷ exterior angle.

mistakes.A: Step 2: divide 360 by the EXTERIOR angle (180 − 144 = 36°), not by the interior angle.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 36° is the exterior angle. Now find how many of them make 360°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the exterior angles add to 360°, not 180°. Divide 360 by 36.

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD and the line bends at E, as shown. ∠ABE = (x + 12)°, ∠CDE = (2x − 6)° and ∠BED = 99°. Find ∠CDE.
questions.explanation: For an arrowhead between parallel lines, the tip angle equals the sum of the arm angles: 3x + 6 = 99, so x = 31 and ∠CDE = 2 × 31 − 6 = 56°. 31 is only x.
steps: Draw a line through E parallel to AB: the tip angle equals the sum of the two arm angles, so (x + 12) + (2x − 6) = 99.
Collect like terms: 3x + 6 = 99, so 3x = 93 and x = 31.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 31 is the value of x. Substitute it into 2x − 6 to find ∠CDE.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 43° is ∠ABE (x + 12). The question asks for ∠CDE = 2x − 6.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the tip angle is not split in half. It equals the sum of the two arm angles: (x + 12) + (2x − 6) = 99.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD with a line bending at E between them, like an arrowhead pointing right. Angle ABE is (x + 12)°, angle CDE is (2x − 6)° and angle BED is 99°

questions.prompt: In the diagram, side QR of triangle PQR is extended to S. ∠P = (x + 15)°, ∠Q = 2x° and the exterior angle ∠PRS = (4x − 25)°. Find ∠PRQ.
questions.explanation: Exterior angle = sum of the interior opposite angles: 4x − 25 = 3x + 15, so x = 40 and ∠PRS = 135°. Then ∠PRQ = 180 − 135 = 45°. 135° is the exterior angle, not the one asked for.
steps: Exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles: 4x − 25 = (x + 15) + 2x = 3x + 15.
Subtract 3x and add 25 to both sides: x = 40, so ∠PRS = 4 × 40 − 25 = 135°.
Angles on a straight line: ∠PRQ = 180 − 135 = 45° (check: 55 + 80 + 45 = 180 ✓).

mistakes.B: Step 3: 135° is the exterior angle ∠PRS. ∠PRQ is the angle inside the triangle next to it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 40 is the value of x, not an angle in the triangle. Substitute it back.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 55° is ∠P (x + 15). The question asks for the interior angle at R.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle PQR with side QR extended past R to S. Angle P is (x + 15)°, angle Q is 2x°, the exterior angle PRS is (4x − 25)°, and angle PRQ is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCD is a rectangle whose diagonals meet at O. ∠DBC = 34°. Find ∠AOB.
questions.explanation: OB = OC, so triangle BOC is isosceles: ∠OCB = 34° and ∠BOC = 180 − 68 = 112°. ∠AOB is on a straight line with ∠BOC, so ∠AOB = 180 − 112 = 68°. 112° is ∠BOC, not ∠AOB.
steps: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, so OB = OC and triangle BOC is isosceles: ∠OCB = ∠OBC = 34°.
Angle sum of triangle BOC: ∠BOC = 180 − 34 − 34 = 112°.
AOC is a straight line, so ∠AOB = 180 − 112 = 68°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 112° is ∠BOC. ∠AOB is next to it on the straight line AC, so subtract from 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 2: ∠OCB is not 90° − 34°. OB = OC, so ∠OCB = ∠OBC = 34°.
mistakes.D: Step 3: ∠AOB is at the crossing point O, not at B. Use triangle BOC and the straight line AC.

questions.diagram_alt: Rectangle ABCD with diagonals meeting at O. Angle DBC (at B, between the diagonal and side BC) is 34°, and angle AOB is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCDEFGH is a regular octagon and the diagonal AC is drawn. Find ∠BAC.
questions.explanation: Each interior angle is 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°, so ∠ABC = 135°. AB = BC, so triangle ABC is isosceles and ∠BAC = (180 − 135) ÷ 2 = 22.5°. 45° forgets to share between the two base angles.
steps: Each interior angle of a regular octagon is (8 − 2) × 180 ÷ 8 = 135°, so ∠ABC = 135°.
AB = BC (regular octagon), so triangle ABC is isosceles with equal base angles at A and C.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 45° is 180° − 135°, the two base angles together. Halve it: there are two equal base angles.
mistakes.B: Step 3: ∠BAC is a base angle of triangle ABC, not half of the 135° interior angle.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 135° is ∠ABC, the octagon's interior angle. ∠BAC is a smaller angle in triangle ABC.

questions.diagram_alt: Regular octagon ABCDEFGH with all sides marked equal and a dashed diagonal AC. Angle BAC is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCD is a kite with AB = AD and CB = CD. ∠BAD = 64° and ∠BCD = 40°. The diagonal BD is drawn. Find ∠DBC.
questions.explanation: In triangle BCD, CB = CD, so the base angles are equal: ∠DBC = (180 − 40) ÷ 2 = 70°. (Check: ∠ABC = (360 − 64 − 40) ÷ 2 = 128° and ∠ABD = 58°, and 128 − 58 = 70 ✓.) 58° is ∠ABD, the wrong triangle.
steps: Look at triangle BCD: CB = CD, so it is isosceles with equal base angles ∠DBC and ∠BDC.
Those two base angles add to 180 − 40 = 140°.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 58° is ∠ABD, in the other triangle (ABD). ∠DBC is in triangle BCD.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 128° is the whole kite angle ∠ABC. The diagonal BD splits it; you want only the part ∠DBC.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 20° is half of ∠BCD. In triangle BCD the equal angles are at B and D, opposite the equal sides CB and CD.

questions.diagram_alt: Kite ABCD with AB = AD (one dash) and CB = CD (two dashes), and dashed diagonal BD. Angle BAD is 64°, angle BCD is 40°, and angle DBC is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: A square and a regular hexagon meet at a point, as shown. The gap between them (marked ?) is exactly filled by one corner of a regular polygon. How many sides does that polygon have?
questions.explanation: The gap is 360 − 90 − 120 = 150°, so the polygon's interior angle is 150°, its exterior angle is 30°, and n = 360 ÷ 30 = 12. 150 is the angle, not the number of sides.
steps: A square corner is 90° and a regular hexagon corner is (6 − 2) × 180 ÷ 6 = 120°.
Angles at a point add to 360°, so the gap is 360 − 90 − 120 = 150° — the polygon's interior angle.
Exterior angle = 180 − 150 = 30°, so n = 360 ÷ 30 = 12 sides.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 150° is the size of the polygon's interior angle, not its number of sides. Keep going.
mistakes.B: Step 3: divide 360 by the EXTERIOR angle (180 − 150 = 30°), not by the interior angle.
mistakes.D: Step 3: n = 360 ÷ exterior angle. 150 ÷ 30 mixes up the interior and exterior angles.
